Modern.brandDescription: Lath & Plaster Interiors is a modern residential and small-commercial interior design practice working primarily in considered renovation of existing buildings.

Lath & Plaster Interiors works across:
• Residential interior design for considered renovations
• Small-commercial design for hospitality and retail clients
• Material-specification consulting for architects

• Studio rental for outside productions
Modern.mission: To make interiors that respect the building they're in.
Modern.vision: A practice whose interiors are documented in books, not on Instagram.
coreValues: Considered — the building is the client.
Modern — heritage is respected, not preserved.
Warm — materials age into the room.
Patient — projects unfold across years, not months.
Modern.brandNameRationale: Lath and Plaster are the two foundational materials in traditional wall construction — wooden strips (lath) finished with plaster. Paired they reference the building tradition before modern drywall. The pairing places the brand firmly in the heritage-renovation tradition. Interiors is the plain category suffix. Stands in the lineage of paired-materials interior practices (Roman & Williams, Studio Sofield).
Modern.manifesto: Most modern interior design practices treat the room as a blank canvas. We started Lath & Plaster because the actual best interiors respect the building they're in — the proportions, the materials, the way the light enters. The practice works on considered renovations, with materials chosen to age into the building rather than impose on it.
Modern.industrySummary: Modern interior design has converged on a soft-modernism aesthetic across magazine publication. The opening is for a practice that works specifically in heritage renovation with material discipline and a print-portfolio register.
Modern.competitorLandscape: Roman & Williams (rwguild.com) holds the closest peer slot in considered heritage interiors. Studio Sofield (studiosofield.com) plays the heritage-residential peer position. Glenn Sestig Architects (glennsestigarchitects.com) sits in the European-heritage middle. Pierre Yovanovitch (pierreyovanovitch.com) is the modern-classical peer reference. We belong alongside Roman & Williams with a tighter material discipline.
Modern.positioningStatement: Lath & Plaster Interiors is a modern interior practice working primarily on heritage renovations with material discipline and a print-portfolio register.
Modern.positioningRationale: We compete on material specification and respect for the existing building. The practice works on a small number of projects per year, documented in printed portfolios.

Creative.brandNameRationale: Reading Light is a phrase about both the literal task lamp and the metaphorical quiet hour in a home. As a brand name it stakes a position about what domestic interior design is actually for. The definite article + Co suffix follows the considered-creative trade-name school (The Pantry Project, The Long Walk Co).
Creative.manifesto: Most interior design treats the room as a magazine spread. We started The Reading Light Co because the actual interesting room is the corner where the client sits at 9pm with a book. Every commission begins with the lamp, the chair, the corner. Everything else is downstream.
Creative.industrySummary: Residential interior design markets on photographs of staged rooms. There is real space for a practice that explicitly designs around use — the reading corner, the kitchen-table evening, the morning window — and publishes work in printed long-form rather than on Instagram.
Creative.competitorLandscape: Studio Ashby (studioashby.com) plays the closest peer in considered residential interiors. Bryan O'Sullivan Studio (bos-studio.com) holds the warm-modern residential slot. Beata Heuman (beataheuman.com) sits in the literary-residential peer position. Roman & Williams (rwguild.com) plays the heritage-residential reference. We sit alongside Beata Heuman with a use-first methodology focus.
Creative.positioningStatement: The Reading Light Co is a residential interior practice that designs rooms around how clients actually use them, beginning with the reading corner.
Creative.positioningRationale: The brand competes on the use-first methodology. Every project begins with the question 'where do you actually sit?' and works outward from the answer.

messagingPillars.name: Use-first methodology
messagingPillars.description: Every project begins with a written documentation of how the client actually uses the rooms — where they sit, when, with what light. The design follows the use.

messagingPillars.name: The reading corner
messagingPillars.description: Every residential project specifies one reading corner as the project's anchor. The lamp, the chair, the table are designed first; the rest of the room follows.

messagingPillars.name: Annual print zine
messagingPillars.description: Once a year the practice publishes a printed zine on domestic light and use — observations from completed projects, lamp specifications, reading-corner photographs.
